headline: Heart Attack Guidelines Finally Account for Women's Health
meta_description: Four major cardiovascular organizations agree on new heart attack definition that corrects decades of under-diagnosis in women through better blood tests and r…
summary_short: Four leading cardiovascular organizations have adopted the first universal heart attack definition, fixing a decades-long diagnostic gap that disproportionately affected…
body:
For the first time, the world's four leading cardiovascular health organizations—the European Society of Cardiology, the American College of Cardiology, the American Heart Association, and the World Heart Federation—have agreed on a single, unified definition of heart attack. The announcement, made at the ESC congress in Munich, includes two critical changes: a reclassification of three heart attack types that occur up to ten times more frequently in women, and a new blood-test threshold that will finally catch cases the old system had been missing in female patients for decades.

The oversight was stark. Three conditions—coronary artery spasm (a stress or cold-triggered tightening of arteries), coronary embolism (a clot blocking an artery), and spontaneous coronary artery dissection, or SCAD (a tear in the artery wall, affecting about 80 percent women, often during or after pregnancy)—had been classified as lower priority than clot-caused heart attacks. Because they ranked lower, women experiencing them often received mismatched or even harmful treatment. Meanwhile, the main diagnostic blood test measuring troponin was calibrated to a single threshold worldwide, one that caught all male heart attacks but systematically missed some women's. Prof. Nicholas Mills of the University of Edinburgh, who led the international task force, called this "unintended systematic bias."

The fix is straightforward in concept but profound in impact: these three conditions now sit alongside traditional heart attacks in the same classification tier, and emergency departments will now apply sex-specific troponin thresholds. Prof. Bryan Williams of the British Heart Foundation noted that "for decades, women have missed out on accurate diagnoses and treatment." Getting four major organizations to align on one global standard was itself a remarkable achievement—published in the European Heart Journal—one that could reshape cardiac care for countless women worldwide.
quick_facts: Four major cardiac organizations agreed on first universal heart attack definition
Three conditions affecting women up to 10 times more common now reclassified
SCAD occurs in about 80 percent of women, often during or after pregnancy
Blood-test threshold had systematically missed heart attacks in female patients
New sex-specific troponin thresholds adopted in emergency departments
